content: 1. Streptomycin should be administered intramuscularly (IM) at a dose of 15 mg/kg every 12 hours for a minimum of 10 days, with a maximum daily dose of 2 g. For children older than 8 years, the dose is 20 mg/kg IM divided every 12 hours for 7–14 days, in combination with tetracycline or co-trimoxazole therapy, with a maximum daily dose of 1 g. 2. Streptomycin enhances the effects of atracurium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 3. Concurrent use of streptomycin and bacitracin increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 4. Streptomycin reduces the efficacy of the BCG live vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. 5. Streptomycin and bumetanide increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, raising the risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 6. Streptomycin reduces the efficacy of the cholera vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid coadministration of systemic antibiotics with the cholera vaccine, as they may act against the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 7. Streptomycin enhances the effects of cisatracurium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 8. Streptomycin and ethacrynic acid increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, raising the risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 9. Streptomycin and furosemide increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, raising the risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 10. Streptomycin reduces the efficacy of oral microbiota products by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibiotics may decrease the efficacy of microbiota products containing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating microbiota therapy. 11. Streptomycin enhances the effects of pancuronium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 12. Quinidine increases the levels or effects of streptomycin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 13. Streptomycin enhances the effects of rapacuronium, rocuronium, and succinylcholine through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 14. Streptomycin and torsemide increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, raising the risk of ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 15. Streptomycin reduces the efficacy of the typhoid live vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. 16. Streptomycin enhances the effects of vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 17. Streptomycin enhances the effects of botulinum toxins (e.g., abobotulinumtoxinA, incobotulinumtoxinA, letibotulinumtoxinA, onabotulinumtoxinA, prabotulinumtoxinA, rimabotulinumtoxinB) through pharmacodynamic synergy. Aminoglycosides may potentiate botulinum toxin effects, leading to excessive neuromuscular weakness and heightened systemic anticholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Streptomycin and amikacin increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Amiodarone increases the levels or effects of streptomycin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Amphotericin B deoxycholate and streptomycin increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 21. Streptomycin reduces the levels or effects of oral conjugated estrogens, estradiol, and other hormonal contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. This interaction poses a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and consider additional forms of birth control. 22. Carboplatin and streptomycin increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Cephalosporins (e.g., cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cefdinir, cefditoren, cefepime, cefixime, cefotaxime, cefotetan, cefoxitin, cefpirome, cefpodoxime, cefprozil, ceftaroline, ceftazidime, ceftibuten, ceftizoxime, ceftobiprole, ceftolozane/tazobactam, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, cephalexin) may increase the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides like streptomycin. Use caution and monitor closely. 24. Cidofovir and streptomycin increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 25. Cisplatin and streptomycin increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. 26. Clarithromycin increases the levels or effects of streptomycin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 27. Clotrimazole decreases the levels or effects of streptomycin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Streptomycin reduces the levels or effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Streptomycin and nephrotoxic agents (e.g., tenofovir, tacrolimus, teicoplanin, tobramycin, colistin, gentamicin, foscarnet) increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 30. Streptomycin increases the levels of peramivir and tenofovir by decreasing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, indomethacin, ketorolac, diclofenac, aspirin) may increase streptomycin levels by decreasing renal clearance, particularly in preterm infants. Use caution and monitor closely. 32. Streptomycin decreases the levels of calcium supplements (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate, calcium chloride, calcium citrate, calcium gluconate) by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 33. Streptomycin decreases the levels of magnesium supplements (e.g., magnesium chloride, magnesium citrate) by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance is unknown. 34. Streptomycin and aztreonam may have synergistic effects against certain bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas spp., Enterobacteriaceae). The clinical significance is unknown. 35. Streptomycin decreases the levels of biotin, cyanocobalamin, and other vitamins by altering gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 36. Streptomycin and St. John’s Wort interact through the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter, potentially reducing streptomycin levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 37. Streptomycin and drugs causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride, sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate) may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Streptomycin and deferasirox increase the risk of acute renal failure. Monitor serum creatinine and renal function closely during coadministration. This summary provides a detailed explanation of streptomycin's interactions with various drugs, emphasizing the need for caution, monitoring, and potential therapy modifications.
